How do I bound lookahead in a hand-rolled HTML scanner?

se-vote-table-never-shown

I am writing a hand-rolled scanner over raw HTML and I keep re-scanning the same tail of the buffer on malformed input. What is the right bound? My working rule is: the scanner must never search the same suffix twice, no matter how many unclosed tags precede it.

A naive version calls indexOf('>') from the current tag-start position every time a candidate tag begins, which is fine for well-formed input but degrades badly once the input contains a long run of unclosed angle brackets with no terminator anywhere nearby.

while (i < len) {
  var j = input.indexOf('>', i);
  if (j === -1) break;
  i = j + 1;
}
homework performance

Track a low-water mark instead of re-searching: remember the position of the last failed search and never let the next scan start before it, even across separate unclosed constructs.

Concretely: keep a single cursor that only moves forward. When a lookahead fails to find its terminator before the end of input, advance the cursor to the end and stop, rather than restarting the search from the next candidate start position — that restart is exactly what turns linear work into quadratic work.

Nice write-up. Worth adding: the same low-water-mark trick applies to unterminated comments and unterminated script/style bodies, not just unclosed tags — anywhere a lookahead can fail to find its terminator.

Agreed, and it is worth instrumenting the bound directly rather than trusting a wall-clock benchmark: count actual scan steps or characters examined per input character, and assert that count stays within a small constant factor as input size grows.

One more edge case worth a test: an attribute value that itself contains an unescaped angle bracket inside a properly quoted string should not confuse the cursor either — the quote-awareness has to compose with the low-water mark, not bypass it.
